doc.title: Bill Kirchner interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2021

title: Joe Wilder, Benny Carter and learning from elders
summary: Kirchner remembers playing at Joe Wilder's memorial and praises Wilder and Benny Carter as gentlemen and teachers who overcame segregation; Wilder was also a photographer.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Thank you for that. We’ve been at this for over an hour so I have two more questions. I saw you perform at Joe Wilder’s memorial service.

Yes. It was very touching and lovely. And I wonder, being friends or associating with gentlemen like Joe from his generation, I’ve had this most marvelous fortunate experience to have a few associations. I wonder what you learned from those guys?

Oh man, well in Joe’s case I mean Joe was the quintessential gentleman in every respect, just the sweetest man and an extraordinary player. But I mean just the way he carried himself. Always had a suit and tie on you know? I mean just the epitome of class, as was somebody else I was fortunate to be able to call a friend and that was Benny Carter, who I got to be good friends with for 25 years. And guys like that, I mean they were just so cool and such great musicians and such great classy people. You know I mean they just lived their lives in such a remarkable way. I mean you couldn’t help, if you had any kind of radar at all you couldn’t help learning stuff from them just because they were great natural teachers. And they set such a great example for so many people. And you know with guys like that, when they came up I mean that was at the height of segregated racist America, I mean some of the stuff that they experienced was frightening I’m sure, but they never let it get them down. They always managed to overcome whatever obstacles that they faced, and triumphed and had great careers and made an enormous difference in the lives of so many of us. I mean for example Benny Carter helped to integrate the two AFM locals in Los Angeles in the early 50s. They combined the black and white locals into one local and Benny was one of the ringleaders in making that come about. So I mean that’s just an example of the impact that he had that went beyond purely musical. But Joe was, I mean he was such a nice man. Always had his camera too.
He was a great photographer. I have a photo of Jackie Cain that he took.
It’s a wonderful photo. I’ll see if I can email it to you.
I’d love that. Thank you. Yeah I was honored one time because he took a picture of me. And I just felt so — it made me feel wonderful.
Oh sure. Yeah. © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-
